questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines an Azure subscription, as distinguished from a resource group or a management group?
options: A billing boundary and an RBAC/Azure Policy scope, tied to exactly one Microsoft Entra tenant
A logical container of resources that share a lifecycle and are deleted together
A container that sits above subscriptions purely to apply RBAC or policy to many subscriptions at once
The top-level management group that every tenant gets automatically, containing everything else
A region-scoped grouping of fault and update domains for VM placement
A JSON file that declares which resources should be deployed
questions.explain: Per Lesson 1, a subscription does two jobs at once: it's a billing boundary (every resource inside rolls up into one invoice) and a scope (RBAC and Policy applied there automatically apply to everything deployed inside it), and every subscription is tied to exactly one Microsoft Entra tenant.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a resource group, not a subscription — resource groups share a lifecycle and are deleted together, but a subscription is specifically the billing boundary and RBAC/Policy scope tied to a Microsoft Entra tenant, one level above resource groups in the hierarchy. Confusing the billing/identity boundary with the lifecycle container is exactly the mix-up Lesson 1 warns against.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every Microsoft Entra tenant automatically has one default, top-level management group called the ________, which contains every other management group and subscription in that tenant.
questions.explain: Per Lesson 1, management groups can be nested up to six levels deep, and every tenant already has one default, top-level management group called the Tenant Root Group, which contains every other management group and subscription automatically.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 2, what does the `--location eastus` on this command actually determine?
options: Only where the resource group's own metadata is stored — resources inside it can still be deployed to any region
That every resource created inside this resource group must also be deployed to East US
The region where Azure Resource Manager itself runs for this subscription
The paired region used automatically for any GRS-replicated storage created in this group
questions.explain: Lesson 2 is explicit that a resource group's `--location` is easy to misread as a constraint on everything inside it, but it isn't — that location only stores the resource group's own metadata, and individual resources inside it can be deployed to any region you choose.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Azure Policy effects, per Lesson 4.
options: A Deny effect blocks a non-compliant deployment outright, at the ARM layer, before the resource is ever created
An Audit effect blocks the deployment but logs who tried to create the resource
An Append effect adds a missing property or setting automatically before deployment
A DeployIfNotExists effect deploys an additional related resource, like a missing diagnostic setting
Policy effects only apply to resources created through the Azure Portal, not the CLI or templates
questions.explain: Deny blocks a deployment outright at the ARM layer; Append adds a missing property automatically; DeployIfNotExists deploys an additional related resource. Audit does the opposite of blocking — it lets the deployment through but flags the resource as non-compliant in reports. And because every tool calls the same ARM API, a policy's effect applies no matter which tool — Portal, CLI, or template — someone used.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the built-in Owner role from the built-in Contributor role in Azure RBAC?
options: Owner has full access to manage resources and can also grant access to other people; Contributor has full access to manage resources but cannot grant access to anyone else
Contributor can grant access to other people, while Owner cannot manage resources directly
Owner can only view resources, while Contributor can create, modify, and delete them
Both roles are functionally identical; they differ only by which scope they can be assigned at
Owner can only be assigned at the resource group scope, while Contributor can be assigned at the management group level
Contributor is a premium role that requires an Entra ID P1 license, while Owner does not
questions.explain: Per Lesson 7, Owner gets full access to everything at the assigned scope, including the ability to grant access to other people. Contributor also gets full access to manage resources — create, modify, delete — but critically cannot grant access to anyone else. That's the one distinction people most often get wrong.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C actually describes the Reader role, not Contributor — Contributor can create, modify, and delete resources just like Owner; the one thing it lacks is the ability to grant access to others. Swapping Contributor's real, full management permissions for Reader's view-only access is exactly the confusion Lesson 7 is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: Match each term from the Azure RBAC role-assignment equation (Lesson 7) to what it actually is.
right: The 'where' — management group, subscription, resource group, or resource — a role applies to
The 'who' in a role assignment — a user, group, service principal, or managed identity
Granting the narrowest role at the narrowest scope that still lets someone do their actual job
The 'what' — a collection of permitted actions, like 'can restart a VM'
questions.explain: Every Azure permission comes down to Role assignment = Security principal + Role definition + Scope. The security principal is the who, the role definition is the what, and scope is the where. Least privilege means granting the narrowest role at the narrowest scope that still does the job — resisting the urge to grant something broader just in case.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Microsoft Entra ID is managed entirely through REST API calls to the ________ API, rather than the LDAP and Kerberos protocols on-prem Active Directory uses.
questions.explain: Per Lesson 5, Entra ID has no domain controllers, no LDAP port, and no Kerberos tickets — it's managed entirely through REST API calls to the Microsoft Graph API over HTTPS, which is why the Azure portal and PowerShell scripts alike are really just making Graph API calls behind the scenes.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Entra ID groups and licensing, per Lesson 6.
options: A security group exists purely to grant access to resources, apps, or Azure RBAC roles, with no collaboration features
A Microsoft 365 group also provisions a shared mailbox, calendar, Teams channel, and SharePoint site
A dynamic group's membership must still be updated manually whenever an attribute like department changes
Group-based licensing means every current member of the group inherits the assigned license automatically
A license is a login credential — without one, a user account cannot sign in at all
questions.explain: A security group is purely an access-control container; a Microsoft 365 group additionally provisions a mailbox, calendar, Teams channel, and SharePoint site. Group-based licensing means members inherit the license automatically — join the group, get the license; leave, lose it. A dynamic group's whole point is that membership maintains itself, with no manual update needed. And a license isn't a login credential — Lesson 6 is explicit that the user account exists and can still sign in without one; a license only unlocks specific services for them.

questions.code:
az vm create \
  --resource-group rg-web-prod \
  --name vm-web01 \
  --image Ubuntu2204 \
  --size Standard_D2s_v5 \
  --admin-username azureuser \
  --generate-ssh-keys
questions.prompt: Per Lesson 9, besides the virtual machine itself, what else does this one command provision by default?
options: An OS disk, a network interface, and — unless told otherwise — a public IP address and a network security group with a default inbound rule
Nothing else; `az vm create` only ever creates the VM resource itself
A full virtual network spanning every region in the subscription
A Virtual Machine Scale Set wrapped around the single VM
questions.explain: Lesson 9 is explicit that a single `az vm create` command provisions a small bundle of resources: the VM itself, an OS disk, a network interface, and — unless told otherwise — a public IP address and an NSG with a default inbound rule (port 22 for Linux, port 3389 for Windows). If no virtual network is specified, Azure creates a default one too.

questions.prompt: Two VMs are placed in the same Availability Set, in different fault domains, inside eastus. A fire destroys the entire datacenter they're both running in. Per Lesson 10, does the Availability Set protect them from this?
options: No — an Availability Set only spreads VMs across fault and update domains inside one datacenter; all VMs in it still go down if that datacenter fails. Availability Zones would have protected them instead
Yes — fault domains guarantee the VMs are placed in physically separate datacenters
Yes — update domains are specifically designed to survive a complete datacenter loss
No — Availability Sets provide no protection of any kind, even against a single rack losing power
questions.explain: Per Lesson 10, an Availability Set's fault and update domains protect against a rack losing power or a maintenance reboot taking out every instance at once, but all VMs in the set still live in the same datacenter. Availability Zones — physically separate datacenters within the region — are the stronger protection that would have survived a whole-datacenter failure.

questions.prompt: Match each VM size family from Lesson 9 to the workload it actually fits.
right: General purpose: balanced CPU-to-memory ratio with no bursting, the default for most production application servers
Compute-optimized: a high CPU-to-memory ratio, fitting batch processing and CPU-heavy workloads
Burstable: a baseline CPU level that accumulates credits to spend bursting above it, good for spiky dev/test loads
Memory-optimized: fits workloads like in-memory caches
questions.explain: B-series is burstable — cheap, with credits for short bursts above a baseline, fitting dev/test and light-traffic boxes. D-series is general purpose with steady performance, the default for production app servers. F-series is compute-optimized for CPU-hungry batch and analytics work. E-series, mentioned briefly, is memory-optimized for workloads like in-memory caches.

questions.prompt: Put Azure Managed Disk's four performance tiers, from Lesson 11, in order from lowest to highest IOPS and cost.
questions.explain: Standard HDD is the cheapest, spinning-disk-backed tier for infrequent access. Standard SSD is SSD-backed with more consistent latency at a still-modest cost. Premium SSD offers high IOPS and low, consistent latency for production databases. Ultra Disk, the top tier, lets you adjust IOPS and throughput independently on the fly for the most demanding workloads.

questions.prompt: A team needs a data disk for a production SQL Server database under heavy I/O load, and a separate place to keep nightly backup files that are rarely read. Per Lessons 11 and 13, which pairing correctly matches workload to tier?
options: Premium SSD (or Ultra Disk) for the SQL data disk; Standard HDD or a Standard-tier storage account for the backups
Standard HDD for the SQL data disk; Premium SSD for the backups
Both should use Ultra Disk, since production workloads always need the top tier regardless of access pattern
Both should use Standard SSD, since it's the one universal default recommended for every workload
questions.explain: Per Lesson 13, Premium is for workloads where latency actually matters, like database disks; Standard is the right default for the bulk of unstructured data like backups and logs where sub-millisecond latency isn't needed. Matching the tier to how much the workload depends on disk speed, not defaulting to one tier for everything, is the point of both lessons.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: of Azure Blob storage's three access tiers, ________ is the cheapest by far but keeps data offline — reading it requires a rehydration request that can take hours.
questions.explain: Per Lesson 14, Archive has the cheapest storage cost of the three tiers, but the data is offline — a rehydration request is required before you can read it, and that can take hours, not milliseconds, which is why it's reserved for data you're unlikely to touch but must retain, often for compliance.

questions.prompt: Match each Azure storage product from Lesson 15 to the storage type it fills.
right: The top-level namespace and billing boundary holding blob, file, queue, and table storage together
File storage: an SMB/NFS share multiple VMs can mount simultaneously
Object storage: HTTP/API access, effectively unlimited scale, many consumers at once
Block storage: raw, fixed-size storage attached to exactly one VM
questions.explain: Blob storage is Azure's object storage. Managed Disks are Azure's block storage, attached to exactly one VM. Azure Files is Azure's file storage, mountable by several VMs at once. All three live inside the storage account, the single management and billing boundary holding blob containers, file shares, queues, and tables underneath it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Azure Storage redundancy options, per Lesson 16.
options: LRS keeps three synchronous copies of data within a single datacenter
ZRS spreads three copies synchronously across separate Availability Zones in the same region
GRS asynchronously replicates an LRS copy to Azure's paired region
ZRS protects against a full regional disaster the same way GRS does
RA-GRS adds read access to the secondary region's copy even while the primary is healthy
questions.explain: LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter; ZRS spreads three copies across Availability Zones in the same region; GRS asynchronously replicates to a paired region; RA-GRS adds readable access to that secondary copy. ZRS never leaves its region, though, so it can't survive a true regional disaster the way GRS can — that protection is exactly what GRS adds over ZRS.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how Azure evaluates Network Security Group (NSG) rules?
options: Rules are evaluated in priority order, lowest number first, and evaluation stops at the first match — a lower-priority number always wins regardless of which rule is more specific
Rules are evaluated by specificity — whichever rule more precisely matches the traffic wins, regardless of priority number
Rules are evaluated in the order they were created, most recent first
All matching rules are applied simultaneously, and a Deny always overrides an Allow regardless of priority
NSG rules are only evaluated for inbound traffic; outbound traffic bypasses NSGs entirely
Priority numbers range from 1 to 100, and higher numbers are evaluated first
questions.explain: Per Lesson 18, Azure evaluates NSG rules in priority order, lowest number first, and stops at the first match. Priority 100 beats priority 200 every time, regardless of which rule is more specific or was written more recently — there's no 'most specific rule wins' logic.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a 'most specific rule wins' model some other firewalls use, but Azure NSGs explicitly don't work that way — Lesson 18 is direct that a lower-priority-number rule always wins over a higher one, even when the higher-priority rule is more specific. Assuming specificity breaks the tie is exactly the mistake that leads to debugging the wrong rule.

questions.prompt: An NSG has a priority-100 rule denying TCP port 22 from everywhere, and a priority-200 rule allowing TCP port 22 from one specific admin IP. Per Lesson 18, does that admin's SSH traffic get through?
options: No — priority 100 is evaluated first, matches, and denies the traffic; the priority-200 Allow rule is never even reached
Yes — the more specific single-IP rule always wins over a broader deny
Yes — Azure merges both rules and allows traffic that either rule permits
It depends on whether the NSG is attached to the subnet or the NIC
questions.explain: Azure evaluates rules lowest-priority-number first and stops at the first match. The priority-100 Deny matches the traffic before the priority-200 Allow is ever evaluated, so the admin's SSH traffic is blocked — exactly the scenario Lesson 18's check-yourself question poses.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Azure reserves ________ IP addresses in every subnet, regardless of size, for its own use — the network address, default gateway, two for DNS, and the broadcast address.
questions.explain: Per Lesson 17, every subnet loses 5 addresses to Azure itself no matter how it's sized, which is the detail that catches people sizing their first small subnet — a /28 with 16 addresses is left with only 11 usable after those 5 reservations.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about VNet peering, per Lesson 20.
options: Peering connects two VNets over Azure's own backbone network, not the public internet
Peering must be created from both sides — a separate link object defined on each VNet
Peering is transitive: if A peers with B, and B peers with C, A can automatically reach C through B
Two VNets with overlapping address spaces can still be peered successfully
Global peering connects VNets in different Azure regions, while regional peering connects VNets in the same region
questions.explain: Peering routes traffic over Azure's backbone rather than the public internet, and has to be created as a pair of link objects, one on each VNet. Global peering crosses regions while regional peering stays within one. Peering is explicitly non-transitive — A peered to B peered to C does not let A reach C — and Azure rejects a peering attempt between VNets whose address spaces overlap.

questions.prompt: A script needs to loop over the names of every VM in a subscription using a shell `for` loop. Per Lesson 21, which `az vm list` output format is the right choice, and why?
options: `--output tsv` — tab-separated with no headers, which a shell loop can iterate over trivially
`--output table` — the human-readable column format is also the easiest for a script to parse
`--output json` — scripts should always parse the richest format available, even for a simple name list
No `--output` flag at all, since `az` commands return plain text by default
questions.explain: Per Lesson 21, `table` is what you reach for while working interactively, `json` is the default every other tool operates on, and `tsv` is what you reach for inside a script because it's trivial to loop over with a shell `for` loop — exactly the use case Lesson 24 puts into practice.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Azure PowerShell ships as a module called ________, the current, cross-platform replacement for the older, retired AzureRM module.
questions.explain: Per Lesson 23, `Az` is installed once per machine and is cross-platform — Windows, macOS, Linux, inside PowerShell 7+ — in a way the deprecated `AzureRM` module never was. Every cmdlet in that lesson comes from `Az`.

questions.prompt: Match each Azure CLI command from Lessons 21-22 to its Azure PowerShell equivalent from Lesson 23.
questions.explain: `az login` opens the same browser sign-in flow as `Connect-AzAccount`. `az account set --subscription` fixes the active subscription exactly like `Set-AzContext`. `az group create` and `New-AzResourceGroup` call the same Resource Manager operation. `az vm list` and `Get-AzVM` both list virtual machines — same underlying ARM calls, two different command syntaxes.

questions.prompt: Put this full CLI resource lifecycle from Lesson 22 in the correct order.
items: az group create — stand up the resource group
az vm create — create the actual resource inside it
az resource list — confirm everything that's really there
az group delete — clean up everything at once
questions.explain: Lesson 22 strings together the full lifecycle an administrator actually runs: create the container first, create the resource inside it, confirm what actually exists with `az resource list` (which shows every resource type, not just VMs), and finally delete the resource group — the one blast-radius boundary that cleans up everything in a single command instead of a scavenger hunt.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes what the Activity Log records from what a platform metric records?
options: The Activity Log records control-plane operations — who did what administrative action and when; a metric is just a numerical measurement like CPU percentage over time, with no identity information at all
A metric records who performed an administrative action, while the Activity Log only stores numerical values
Both record exactly the same data; the Activity Log is simply the metric data exported to a storage account
The Activity Log only tracks failed operations, while metrics track successful ones
Metrics are retained for 90 days and the Activity Log for 93 days, but they otherwise record identical information
The Activity Log requires an agent installed on every VM, while metrics are collected automatically
questions.explain: Per Lesson 26, the Activity Log records control-plane operations — who did it, what operation ran, when, and whether it succeeded — against Azure Resource Manager. A metric, per Lesson 25, is just a numerical value like CPU percentage with no identity information, which is exactly why a metric chart could show a VM is off but never show who turned it off.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E gets the retention numbers backwards and still misses the real distinction — platform metrics are retained 93 days by default and the Activity Log 90 days, but the point Lesson 26 actually makes isn't about retention length at all. It's that only the Activity Log captures the caller's identity; a metric like CPU percentage was never going to tell you who stopped a VM no matter how long it's kept.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Azure Monitor alert rules and Action Groups, per Lesson 27.
options: An alert rule is built from a condition (what to watch for) and an action (what happens when it's true)
An Action Group is defined once and can be attached to many different alert rules
Severity determines whether an alert rule fires, not just how it's triaged afterward
A condition's evaluation frequency and time window exist specifically to avoid firing on a brief, normal spike
An Action Group can only send email; webhooks and automation runbooks aren't supported
questions.explain: An alert rule is a condition plus an action, and an Action Group is a separate, reusable object attached to as many alert rules as needed. The evaluation window — like 'over 80% for 5 minutes' — exists specifically so a brief, normal spike doesn't trigger a noisy, useless alert. Severity doesn't change whether a rule fires at all, only how it's triaged afterward, and Action Groups support email, SMS, webhooks, Azure Functions, Logic Apps, and automation runbooks — not just email.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: once log data lands in a Log Analytics workspace, you search it using ________ — the same query language that also powers Microsoft Sentinel.
questions.explain: Per Lesson 26, KQL (Kusto Query Language) is the language you write against a Log Analytics workspace, and it isn't specific to Log Analytics — it's the exact same query language that powers Microsoft Sentinel, Azure's cloud SIEM.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Briarcliff's multi-tier environment build, from Lesson 29, in the order they were actually done.
items: Create a tagged resource group (environment, costcenter, owner)
Create a VNet split into a web subnet and an app subnet
Create the web-tier VM with a public IP in the web subnet
Create the app-tier VM with no public IP in the app subnet
Create a storage account for application data
questions.explain: Lesson 29 builds the environment in exactly this order: the tagged resource group first (so everything created afterward is already governed), then the VNet shaped into its two subnets, then the web VM with a public IP since customers need to reach it, then the app VM deliberately withheld from a public IP, and finally a storage account for data that shouldn't live only on a VM's local disk.

questions.prompt: Briarcliff's budget alert fires at 80% of its $150 monthly budget on day 19. Per Lesson 31, what two separate cost problems does the cost-by-resource breakdown reveal about `loadtest-vm1`, and what's the fix for each?
options: An oversized Standard_D4s_v3 VM left running since a load test, and a Premium_LRS disk attached to it — fixed by deallocating and resizing the VM down, and dropping the disk to StandardSSD_LRS
An expired Azure Policy assignment and a missing tag — fixed by reapplying the policy and adding the tag
A VNet peering misconfiguration causing duplicate billing — fixed by deleting one of the peering links
A Conditional Access policy blocking sign-ins — fixed by excluding the VM's service principal from the policy
questions.explain: Per Lesson 31, `loadtest-vm1` is a Standard_D4s_v3 — far bigger than anything else in the environment — left running continuously since a load test two weeks earlier, with a Premium_LRS disk attached despite only ever being meant for a one-off test. The fix deallocates and resizes the VM to Standard_B2s and drops the disk to StandardSSD_LRS, matching the resource to what it's actually for.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how Briarcliff's environment was built and secured across Lessons 29-30.
options: The app-tier VM (app-vm1) was created with no public IP at all, so it's never directly reachable from the internet
app-nsg's allow rule sources traffic from 10.20.1.0/24 (the web subnet), not from the Internet service tag
The ops team's Virtual Machine Contributor role was assigned at the subscription scope, not the resource group
The budget's 80% alert threshold on a $150 monthly budget works out to $120
web-vm1 and app-vm1 both use the Standard_D4s_v3 VM size
questions.explain: `app-vm1` was created with `--public-ip-address ""`, deliberately never internet-facing, and `app-nsg`'s allow rule trusts only `10.20.1.0/24` — the web subnet — not the Internet. Eighty percent of a $150 budget is $120, which is the line Lesson 30 sets and Lesson 31 crosses. The ops team's role was scoped to `briarcliff-rg` specifically, not the subscription, and both VMs use the modest, burstable `Standard_B2s`, not `Standard_D4s_v3` (that oversized size belongs to the unrelated `loadtest-vm1` from Lesson 31).
